T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers use health data as a social signal of achievement and commitment; a branded, high‑end device becomes a visible marker of personal health dedication.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita sells through design‑focused retailers and online marketplaces at premium prices, leveraging the device’s aesthetic appeal and brand prestige to command higher margins.
assumptions: Consumers associate health data with social status and are willing to pay for visible health credentials.
Tanita can design a consumer‑friendly version that is aesthetically appealing and easy to use.
Specialty retailers and online marketplaces will stock a premium health device.

Each participant receives a branded home body‑fat analyzer (Tanita model) and a product description emphasizing either (a) medical evidence and personal health management (functional messaging) or (b) status signaling and commitment to wellness (status messaging). X1.sample: 1,000 health‑conscious adults, recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and gender.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: purchase intent (binary) after 12 weeks. Secondary outcomes: willingness to pay a premium price (e.g., 20% above standard retail price) and repeat purchase rate for subscription services.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent under functional versus status messaging before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious adults (aged 25–55) who already track body composition and are willing to pay a premium for clinically validated health tools.
final.value_proposition: A branded home body‑fat analyzer that leverages Tanita’s medical‑grade bioelectrical impedance technology, positioned as a reliable personal health monitor for functional health management.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 1,000 health‑conscious adults, randomizing between functional and status messaging, and measure purchase intent, willingness to pay, and repeat purchase rate.
final.uncertainty: Consumer demand for a premium home body‑fat analyzer is uncertain; evidence shows widespread household ownership of bathroom scales in Japan but does not prove willingness to pay a premium for a branded device.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for status messaging exceeds functional messaging by at least 10 percentage points, we would shift focus to a status‑driven proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness, or a niche market) and not general market trends.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into new customer segments (e.g., leisure boating, commercial fishing) without a differentiated consumer proposition.
3) Maintain the current product portfolio and not pursue any expansion (no expansion).
4) License the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, emergency-proven safety solution that can be used in remote, high-risk environments.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, paddlers) who need a device that can be used in isolation and that SAR services recognize and can locate.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The FCC legalizing PLBs in 2002 and the proven success of PLBs in saving lives (e.g., 230 outdoor enthusiasts) create a perceived safety benefit that justifies purchase.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by selling the GyPSI 406 PLB directly to consumers through retail channels, charging a premium for a trusted, FCC-approved device.
assumptions: Outdoor recreationists are willing to pay for safety equipment that has been proven effective.
The 406 MHz frequency is reliable and can be detected by SAR services.
Retail distribution channels exist and are willing to stock a consumer-oriented PLB.
predictions: If ACR launches a consumer proposition targeting outdoor recreation, purchase intent among surveyed hikers will be at least 15% higher than for a generic PLB.
Sales of the GyPSI 406 will increase in regions with high outdoor recreation activity (e.g., national parks) relative to low-activity regions.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, emergency-proven safety solution that can be used in remote, high-risk environments.

T2.claim: Emergency services and outdoor recreation organizations will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, SAR-compatible solution that can be integrated into existing search and rescue protocols and used for group safety.
T2.who_benefits: Search and rescue agencies (e.g., FEMA, local SAR teams) and outdoor recreation organizations (national parks, hiking clubs) that need a standardized, detectable distress signal for remote areas.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The FCC legalizing PLBs and the proven success of PLBs in saving lives (e.g., 230 outdoor enthusiasts) create a perceived safety benefit that justifies procurement by public agencies and organizations.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by selling the GyPSI 406 PLB through government contracts and B2B channels, charging a premium for a trusted, FCC-approved device that meets SAR standards.
assumptions: Emergency services prioritize devices that can be detected by SAR satellites.
Outdoor recreation organizations are willing to adopt a device that integrates with existing SAR protocols.
Government procurement processes allow for testing and approval of new PLB models.
predictions: If ACR offers a consumer proposition that emphasizes SAR compatibility and integration with outdoor recreation groups, procurement inquiries from SAR agencies will increase by at least 10% compared to a generic PLB.
Sales of the GyPSI 406 will be higher in regions with active SAR teams and outdoor recreation facilities than in low-activity areas.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.

assumptions: Outdoor recreationists are willing to pay for safety equipment that has been proven effective.
The 406 MHz frequency is reliable and can be detected by SAR services.
Retail distribution channels exist and are willing to stock a consumer-oriented PLB.

result.excerpt: The 406 MHz PLB is primarily intended to provide a distress and alerting capacity for use by the general public in life threatening situations in a remote environment after all other means of notifying SAR responders (e.g., telephone, radio) have been exhausted.

arguments.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, emergency-proven safety solution that can be used in remote, high-risk environments.
arguments.who_benefits: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, paddlers) who need a device that can be used in isolation and that SAR services recognize and can locate.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: The FCC legalizing PLBs in 2002 and the proven success of PLBs in saving lives (e.g., 230 outdoor enthusiasts) create a perceived safety benefit that justifies purchase.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by selling the GyPSI 406 PLB directly to consumers through retail channels, charging a premium for a trusted, FCC-approved device.
assumptions: Outdoor recreationists are willing to pay for safety equipment that has been proven effective.
The 406 MHz frequency is reliable and can be detected by SAR services.
Retail distribution channels exist and are willing to stock a consumer-oriented PLB.
predictions: If ACR launches a consumer proposition targeting outdoor recreation, purchase intent among surveyed hikers will be at least 15% higher than for a generic PLB.
Sales of the GyPSI 406 will increase in regions with high outdoor recreation activity (e.g., national parks) relative to low-activity regions.

arguments.claim: Emergency services and outdoor recreation organizations will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, SAR-compatible solution that can be integrated into existing search and rescue protocols and used for group safety.
arguments.who_benefits: Search and rescue agencies (e.g., FEMA, local SAR teams) and outdoor recreation organizations (national parks, hiking clubs) that need a standardized, detectable distress signal for remote areas.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: The FCC legalizing PLBs and the proven success of PLBs in saving lives (e.g., 230 outdoor enthusiasts) create a perceived safety benefit that justifies procurement by public agencies and organizations.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by selling the GyPSI 406 PLB through government contracts and B2B channels, charging a premium for a trusted, FCC-approved device that meets SAR standards.
assumptions: Emergency services prioritize devices that can be detected by SAR satellites.
Outdoor recreation organizations are willing to adopt a device that integrates with existing SAR protocols.
Government procurement processes allow for testing and approval of new PLB models.
predictions: If ACR offers a consumer proposition that emphasizes SAR compatibility and integration with outdoor recreation groups, procurement inquiries from SAR agencies will increase by at least 10% compared to a generic PLB.
Sales of the GyPSI 406 will be higher in regions with active SAR teams and outdoor recreation facilities than in low-activity areas.

arguments.quote: The 406 MHz PLB is primarily intended to provide a distress and alerting capacity for use by the general public in life threatening situations in a remote environment after all other means of notifying SAR responders (e.g., telephone, radio) have been exhausted.
arguments.does_not_show: It does not show that outdoor recreation enthusiasts will purchase the device or that they perceive it as a reliable safety solution.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Government Proposition Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation group receiving a consumer-focused description of the GyPSI 406 PLB emphasizing proven rescues, reliability, and retail availability. (B) Emergency services/outdoor recreation group receiving a government/B2B description of the same device emphasizing SAR compatibility, integration with protocols, and procurement channels. Both groups view the same product
arguments.sample: 500 participants: 250 outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, campers) recruited via outdoor forums; 250 public safety/SAR personnel recruited via professional networks. Stratify by region to include areas with high outdoor recreation activity and active SAR teams.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1=Very unlikely, 7=Very likely) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: perceived reliability (1-10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show purchase intent ≥5.5 and willingness to pay ≥€300, while Group B will show lower intent (below 5).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show purchase intent ≥5.5 and willingness to pay ≥€300, while Group A will show lower intent (below 5).

arguments.decision_rule: If Group A mean purchase intent ≥5.5 and willingness to pay ≥€300, proceed with consumer proposition targeting outdoor recreation. If Group B mean purchase intent ≥5.5 and willingness to pay ≥€300, proceed with government/B2B proposition. If both groups meet

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue monitoring market demand and consider a low-cost test of consumer purchase intent before committing resources.

arguments.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, campers, paddlers) and emergency services/outdoor recreation organizations that need a reliable, SAR-compatible distress beacon.
arguments.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that is proven effective in saving lives, compliant with FCC regulations, and marketed as a consumer product through retail channels.
arguments.next_action: Run a low-cost online survey (e.g., 500 participants, €15,000 budget, 10 weeks) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a consumer-focused GyPSI 406 PLB.
arguments.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand or willingness to pay. The FCC legalizing PLBs in 2002 and proven rescues do not prove that outdoor recreationists will adopt the device.
would_change_if: If the survey shows purchase intent ≥5.5 and willingness to pay ≥€300 for a consumer proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer product.
If a separate survey shows procurement intent ≥5.5 and willingness to pay ≥€300 for a government/B2B proposition, explore that route.
If both survey results meet thresholds, consider a dual-track approach.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue monitoring market demand and gather real-world evidence before committing resources. The evidence base is limited to regulatory intent and a few anecdotal success stories; it does not show consumer purchase intent or agency procurement behavior in 2002. A small pilot test (e.g., the proposed consumer vs agency pilot) would be the next step,

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness, or a niche market) and not general market trends.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into new customer segments (e.g., leisure boating, commercial fishing) without a differentiated consumer proposition.
3) Maintain the current product portfolio and not pursue any expansion (no expansion).
4) License the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz PLBs because they provide a reliable distress signal in remote areas where other communication methods fail.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, paddlers) who need emergency backup in remote locations.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The FCC rule allowing PLB use in the continental U.S. (2002) and the proven success of PLBs in saving lives (e.g., 230 outdoor enthusiasts saved) create a perceived safety benefit that outweighs cost.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can charge a premium price for a specialized consumer product, sell through outdoor retailers, and potentially offer subscription services for battery replacement.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large enough to support a dedicated consumer product.
Consumers trust the FCC approval and PLB reliability for emergency use.
Distribution channels (retailers, outdoor gear stores) are accessible to ACR.
predictions: If ACR launches a consumer-focused PLB, purchase intent among outdoor recreationists will be above 10% in a survey.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with high outdoor recreation participation (e.g., national parks, hiking trails).
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz PLBs because they provide a reliable distress signal in remote areas where other communication methods fail.

T2.claim: Emergency services and outdoor recreation agencies will adopt 406 MHz PLBs to reduce search and rescue time and cost, leading to institutional procurement.
T2.who_benefits: Search and rescue agencies (e.g., National Park Service, state parks, emergency management), and potentially outdoor recreation organizations that provide safety equipment to members.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The FCC rule allowing PLB use and the proven success of PLBs in saving lives (e.g., 230 outdoor enthusiasts saved) create a perceived cost savings and efficiency improvement for agencies that currently rely on other methods.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell through government procurement channels, offer volume discounts, and potentially bundle PLBs with other safety equipment for agencies.
assumptions: Government procurement cycles for safety equipment are active in 2002.
Agencies prioritize cost reduction and efficiency in search and rescue.
Distribution channels to agencies (e.g., state procurement offices) are accessible to ACR.
predictions: If ACR offers a consumer-focused PLB to agencies, procurement inquiries will exceed 5 per month.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with high outdoor recreation activity and active search and rescue programs.
T2.first_claim: Emergency services and outdoor recreation agencies will adopt 406 MHz PLBs to reduce search and rescue time and cost, leading to institutional procurement.

X1.method: Run two parallel pilot programs in the same geographic area (e.g., a national park and surrounding outdoor recreation areas). In the consumer pilot, ACR markets a consumer-focused 406 MHz PLB through outdoor retailers and online channels, offering a limited-time discount and promotional materials emphasizing emergency distress capability in remote areas. In the agency pilot, ACR offers the same PLB to search and rescue agencies and outdoor recreation organizations at a volume discount, emphasizing cost savings and efficiency improvements. Both pilots
X1.sample: Consumer pilot: 500 units sold through 10 outdoor retailers over 12 weeks. Agency pilot: 200 units distributed to 10 search and rescue agencies and outdoor recreation organizations over 12 weeks.
X1.measure: Consumer pilot: units sold, conversion rate (sales/visits), average price paid. Agency pilot: number of inquiries, purchase orders placed, average price per unit.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Consumer pilot will achieve a conversion rate of at least 10% and average price paid above €300; agency pilot will generate fewer than 5 inquiries per month.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Agency pilot will receive at least 15 purchase orders and average price per unit below €400; consumer pilot will generate fewer than 500 units sold.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue monitoring market demand and gather real-world evidence before committing resources. The evidence base is limited to regulatory intent and a few anecdotal success stories; it does not show consumer purchase intent or agency procurement behavior in 2002. A small pilot test (e.g., the proposed consumer vs agency pilot) would be the next step.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, campers, paddlers) who need emergency backup in remote locations
final.value_proposition: A specialized 406 MHz PLB marketed through outdoor retailers, offering a reliable distress signal in remote areas, with a premium price justified by FCC approval and proven survival success.
final.next_action: Run a limited pilot (e.g., 500 units in 10 outdoor retailers over 12 weeks) to test consumer demand and conversion rate. Use the results to decide whether to scale the consumer proposition.
final.uncertainty: Consumer demand for a 406 MHz PLB is uncertain due to lack of direct purchase data; agency procurement behavior is also uncertain due to limited evidence of institutional adoption.
would_change_if: If the pilot achieves a conversion rate of at least 10% and average price paid above €300, the consumer proposition becomes more likely.
If the pilot generates at least 15 purchase orders and average price per unit below €400, the institutional procurement proposition becomes more likely.
If neither condition is met, the recommendation remains to not invest until more evidence is gathered.

Begin with a limited launch in outdoor retail channels, priced at €350, and measure purchase intent and willingness to pay through a targeted survey before scaling. The evidence shows regulatory approval for general public use, existing outdoor rescue success stories, and a clear safety‑‑‑

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness, or a niche market) and not general market trends.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into new customer segments (e.g., leisure boating, commercial fishing) without a differentiated consumer proposition.
3) Maintain the current product portfolio and not pursue any expansion (no expansion).
4) License the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment.
T1.who_benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.
assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.
Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.
Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.
predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.
Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a status symbol and status-driven purchase, because they associate the tractor with modern, affluent lifestyle and community recognition.
T2.who_benefits: Affluent households and early adopters who use lawn care as a way to signal social status and modern living.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers seek products that convey prestige and align with their social circle. A tractor that is marketed as a stylish, innovative tool becomes a visible marker of affluence.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price the tractor at a premium, sell branded apparel and accessories, and build a community around ownership, creating a lifestyle brand that commands higher margins.
assumptions: Status is a primary purchase driver for a segment of small‑holder households.
Modern, aesthetically pleasing design is valued over purely functional features.
Deere can design a tractor that is visually distinctive without compromising performance.
predictions: In a test offering a status‑oriented tractor at a price above comparable functional models, purchase intent among affluent respondents will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a purely functional tractor.
Willingness to pay for a status‑oriented tractor will be at least 15% higher than for a comparable functional model.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment.
arguments.who_benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.
assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.
Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.
Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.
predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.
Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model.

Deere can design a tractor that is visually distinctive without compromising performance.
predictions: In a test offering a status‑oriented tractor at a price above comparable functional models, purchase intent among affluent respondents will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a purely functional tractor.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.
assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.
Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.
Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.
predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.
Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product concepts: (1) a functional, multi‑purpose lawn and garden tractor emphasizing affordability, practicality, and versatility; (2) a status‑oriented tractor emphasizing modern design, prestige, and community recognition. Participants will be asked about purchase intent and willingness to pay for each concept.
arguments.sample: 500 small‑holder households (households with small gardens and limited storage) recruited via an online panel, stratified by income and geographic region.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" vs. "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (EUR amount).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the functional, multi‑purpose tractor compared to the status‑oriented tractor.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the status‑oriented tractor compared to the functional, multi‑purpose tractor.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two concepts exceeds 10 percentage points in favor of the functional tractor, we conclude evidence supports T1. result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.target_customer: Small‑holder households with limited storage and budget, who currently use multiple tools for yard tasks.
arguments.value_proposition: A compact, multi‑purpose lawn and garden tractor that performs several tasks (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) at a price comparable to a single‑purpose tool, reducing tool count and maintenance costs.
arguments.next_action: Run a 12‑week pilot offering a functional, multi‑purpose tractor to 200 small‑holder households at a price 10‑15% above a comparable single‑purpose model. Measure purchase intent and willingness to pay.
arguments.uncertainty: Demand for a differentiated consumer product is uncertain due to lack of direct evidence of consumer behavior and willingness to pay. The pilot will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows purchase intent for the multi‑purpose tractor exceeding 15% over a single‑purpose model, or willingness to pay at least 10% higher, we would shift to a full consumer launch.
If the pilot shows no significant difference or negative response, we would abandon the consumer proposition and remain focused on B2B.

constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline are analyst assumptions for evaluating evidence.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, hobby gardening, or a niche agricultural task) using existing tractor engineering.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.
assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.
Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.
Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.
predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.

Half see a functional description emphasizing affordability and practicality; half see a status‑oriented description emphasizing modern design, prestige, and community signaling. After viewing, participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point
X1.sample: 200 U.S. households with small gardens (under 0.5 acres) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and region.
X1.measure: Mean WTP in euros for each version. Secondary measure: purchase intent (binary: would buy within 6 months).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Mean WTP for the functional version will be at least 10% higher than for the status version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Mean WTP for the status version will be at least 10% higher than for the functional version.

X1.decision_rule: If functional WTP ≥ status WTP + 10% → adopt T1; else if status WTP ≥ functional WTP + 10% → adopt T2; else inconclusive.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized product presentation. Participants view a mock 1962 lawn and garden tractor described as a versatile, low‑cost tool for multiple yard tasks. Half see a functional description emphasizing affordability and practicality; half see a status‑oriented description emphasizing modern design, prestige, and community signaling. After viewing, participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point
arguments.sample: 200 U.S. households with small gardens (under 0.5 acres) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and region.
arguments.measure: Mean WTP in euros for each version. Secondary measure: purchase intent (binary: would buy within 6 months).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Mean WTP for the functional version will be at least 10% higher than for the status version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Mean WTP for the status version will be at least 10% higher than for the functional version.

arguments.decision_rule: If functional WTP ≥ status WTP + 10% → adopt T1; else if status WTP ≥ functional WTP + 10% → adopt T2; else inconclusive.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on the existing B2B dealer network and existing product lines. Conduct a limited pilot test of a functional, low‑cost multi‑purpose tractor to validate demand before scaling.
